sources.title: Abay Kunanbaiuly (Q304890), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-18): English label 'Abay Kunanbaiuly', description 'Kazakh poet, philosopher and composer (1845-1904)', instance of human, born 29 July 1845 (Wikidata) and died 23 June 1904, citizen of the Russian Empire, Korean label 아바이 쿠난바이울리. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

George Kennan, 'Siberia and the Exile System', vol. 1 (New York: The Century Co., 1891), the Semipalatinsk chapter around pp. 183-185 (Internet Archive scan, OCR text read for the passage and its context). CONTEMPORARY OUTSIDE ACCOUNT, SECOND-HAND: at a dinner of political exiles in 1885 an exile, Leontiev, tells Kennan of 'a learned old Kirghis here, named Ibrahim Konobai' who uses the library and reads Buckle, Mill and Draper, who once asked him the difference between induction and deduction, and whom he examined for two evenings on Draper's 'Intellectual Development of Europe' and found to have 'a very fair comprehension'. Kennan never met him; researchers identify the man with Abai, which the book does not state.

Alikhan Bukeikhanov, 'Abai (Ibrahim) Kunanbayev', obituary first printed in Semipalatinsky Listok in 1905 (English translation on the site of the Abai Institute, Al-Farabi Kazakh National University; read in full; the translation is rough). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: the first biographical account, by a Kazakh contemporary who says some details came from Abai's circle: his education at the Semipalatinsk madrasa and three months at a Russian school, his work with his father in steppe disputes, his reading of Russian writers and of Spencer, Lewes and Draper after meeting the exiles Michaelis and Gross, his translations of Lermontov, Krylov and Pushkin (including Tatiana's letter, which a Kokand singer performed to the author in 1899), his sending his second son to a Tyumen school and on to St Petersburg at his own cost, his regret at not studying earlier, his later withdrawal from public affairs and his death weeks after his son Magauiya in 1904; it also says his poems were to be collected by his son Turagul.

Abai Institute (Kazakhstan), 'Biography of Abay Kunanbayev' (oq.gov.kz, material adapted from the online encyclopedia abaialemi.kz; read in full). OFFICIAL AND HAGIOGRAPHIC: his clan and education, election as volost head in 1875-78 and chief judge in 1885, drafting of regulations on crimes in three days, a seven-year feud with Orazbai from 1891 and an attempt on his life in 1898, the first signed poem in 1886, the Words of Edification in forty-six chapters, songs, readings in Russian and Western authors, and rhetorical claims (his translations 'sometimes surpassed the originals') that are not repeated here. The page chrome includes an AI chat widget, which was ignored.

K. Iskakov, 'Life of Abai (Ibragim) Kunanbaev' (Abai Institute site, Al-Farabi Kazakh National University, 2012; read in full). A longer narrative biography in English translation that closely follows Bukeikhanov and Auezov: his father's rule and education policy, his early satire, the friendship with the exiles Michaelis and Gross, the reading list, translations of Lermontov, Pushkin and Krylov, his schooling of his sons (second son to Tyumen real school at about a hundred rubles a year, died 1895), poems on his isolation and enemies in 1886-91 (translated by McKane and Shartse), and the death of his son Magauiya in 1904. Derivative of the earlier accounts, so not an independent second family.

Asur Ozdemir (Khoja Ahmed Yasawi International Kazakh-Turkish University), 'Kazak edebi dilinin kurucusu, Kazaklar'in klasik sairi Abay (Ibrahim) Kunanbayuli (1845-1904)' (Turkish-language academic article, translated with notes from K. Alpisbay's Kazakh literature textbook, Almaty 1992; read in full in Turkish). Covers his reading, his 1889 translation of eight Onegin passages, his satires on officials ('I became a volost ruler' and 'Your ruler rejoices'), his poem on the internat criticising the tsarist system of administration and education, publication of his early verses under his pupil Kokbay's name until 1886, and his metrical and rhyme innovations (cross rhyme, paired rhyme, mixed rhyme). Textbook-derived and admiring.

Iraj Bashiri (University of Minnesota), 'A brief note on the life of Abai Kunanbaev' (2000; read in full). Short Western academic summary: his Russian education, his satires 'Kulembaiu' (1888), 'Luckily, I too became a governor' (1889) and 'The bailiff delights in authority' (1889), the seasons poems, the ballads 'Mas'ud' and 'Alexander', his songs, and Mukhtar Auezov's two novels about him; says Soviet commentators favoured him as an emblem of progress and that Auezov's saga is a source for the story of his decision to 'civilise' the Kazakhs, i.e. a literary rather than documentary account.

Kazinform (MIA), 'Kak byl izdan pervyi sbornik stikhov Abaya' (How the first collection of Abai's poems was published), 10 February 2020 (read in Russian). Reports that after his death in 1904 his nephew Kakitai and son Turagul collected his poems, which Bukeikhanov had urged, and that the first collection was printed in St Petersburg in 1909; it also quotes the memoir of the son of Aniyar Moldabaev, kept at the Abai museum, that Abai sent the orphaned boy to a boarding school in Semey and later helped raise money to buy him a house. Regional news article; the memoir is a family source.

Sanzhar Syrgabayev, 'Depicting Abai: how the canonical image of the poet was created', Qalam, 9 January 2026 (read for the history of his portraits; not used for any trait row). Says the earliest portrait is P. D. Lobanovsky's 1887 drawing made in Semipalatinsk in the poet's lifetime, that the 'famous photograph of Abai with his sons' reached the Semipalatinsk museum only on 6 February 1941 (donated by Mukhtar Auezov, receipt no. 40, after being given to Auezov by the writer Manap Moldabaev in 1933), and that artists of the 1934 portrait competition worked from it.

curiosity.rationale: [src_abai_kennan, src_abai_bukeikhanov, src_abai_ozdemir, src_abai_iskakov | 1870s-1904 | contemporary outside account, contemporary Kazakh obituary, academic article, narrative biography] Two contemporary accounts agree on a self-directed reading programme beyond the steppe: the exile Leontiev told Kennan in 1885 of an old Kazakh who read Buckle, Mill and Draper and asked him to explain induction and deduction, and Bukeikhanov lists Spencer, Lewes and Draper alongside the Russian writers and says he taught himself Arabic and Persian. CONCENTRATION CHECK: Kennan's account is second-hand and does not name Abai, Bukeikhanov's English text is rough, and the later biographies repeat Bukeikhanov. Lowered from 78 / 0.64 to 74 / 0.60.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_abai_bukeikhanov, src_abai_kazinform, src_abai_iskakov | 1880s-1895 | contemporary Kazakh obituary, regional news article quoting a family memoir, narrative biography] Bukeikhanov says he paid for his second son's schooling in Tyumen and St Petersburg and calls him the first Kazakh to sacrifice so much for a child's education, and a memoir of Aniyar Moldabaev's son says Abai sent the orphaned boy to a boarding school in Semey and helped fund a house for him. His verse states the aim of improving the reader's mind. Reviewed in the concentration check and kept: two distinct kinds of act, from a contemporary and from a separate family memoir; the verse is self-statement and is not counted as behaviour.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_abai_bukeikhanov, src_abai_ozdemir, src_abai_bashiri, src_abai_institute | 1880s | contemporary Kazakh obituary, academic article, Western academic note, official biography] He satirised the akyn singers who flattered the rich and the officials of his day (the 1887 and 1889 poems; Bukeikhanov and Ozdemir) and criticised the tsarist administration and the boarding-school system in verse (Ozdemir); his religious conduct is described inconsistently (one account says he kept Ramadan and was lax in daily prayer, another that he did not observe fasting), so it is not used. CONCENTRATION CHECK: nearly all of this is his own verse as read by a national-literature tradition, with no independent observer of how he argued in person; lowered from 68 / 0.52 (strong inference) to 62 / 0.46 (inference).

creative_originality.rationale: [src_abai_ozdemir, src_abai_bukeikhanov, src_abai_bashiri | 1880s-1899 | academic article, contemporary Kazakh obituary, Western academic note] Ozdemir lists new rhyme patterns (cross, paired and mixed rhyme) that he says Abai introduced after translating Pushkin, Bashiri says the four-seasons poems have 'innovative features', and Bukeikhanov records that by 1899 singers across the steppe were performing his Russian translations. CONCENTRATION CHECK: the originality claims come from one textbook-derived family and an admiring tradition, and no outside scholar of verse form is cited; lowered from 70 / 0.52 (strong inference) to 64 / 0.44 (inference).

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_abai_bukeikhanov, src_abai_institute, src_abai_iskakov | 1885-1904 | contemporary Kazakh obituary, official biography, narrative biography] Bukeikhanov says he entered the contest between clan parties in his thirties and then withdrew to a quieter life; the official biography adds a seven-year feud with Orazbai from 1891 and a letter to the Senate, and his poems of 1886-91 speak of enemies and of seclusion. SELF-CALIBRATION: lowered from 62 / 0.46 to 56 / 0.38 because the feud rests on a single official source and the sources disagree on how involved he stayed in public affairs.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_abai_bashiri, src_abai_institute, src_abai_bukeikhanov | 1870s-1904 | Western academic note, official biography, contemporary Kazakh obituary] He wrote lyric and narrative poetry, composed songs, translated Russian poets and wrote a prose work of reflections, and the official biography adds the 1885 legal regulations. Most of it lies within literature and its adjacent arts, and the songs and prose are described chiefly by later official sources. SELF-CALIBRATION: lowered from 64 / 0.48 to 56 / 0.40.

portrait.source: The seated figure of Abai cropped from the well-known photograph of Abai with his sons (the only authentic photograph of him known to scholarship), as held on Wikimedia Commons as 'Abai Kunanbaev.jpg' (1085 x 1460, a 2020 crop with a levels adjustment by a Commons editor from a 1852 x 2460 scan taken from a baq.kz news page); downscaled to 743 x 1000, no upscaling, greyscale as supplied. Published scholarship (Qalam, 2026, citing the museum receipt and the journal 'Abai', 1995, no. 3) says the photograph was given to Mukhtar Auezov by the writer Manap Moldabaev in 1933 and was registered in the Semipalatinsk Abai museum on 6 February 1941 (receipt no. 40, donated by Auezov), and describes the sitter's frontal pose, vertical-striped chapan and skullcap, which the crop shows.
portrait.license: Public domain by age: a photograph taken no later than 1904 (the sitter's death), photographer not named in any source read, so it is an anonymous work more than 120 years old; first publication is not documented (circulating from 1933). No holder rights statement was reachable, and the Commons PD-old template alone is not relied on
portrait.attribution: Photographer unknown, undated (made before 1904); photograph of Abai with his sons, Abai Museum, Semey (per Qalam); Wikimedia Commons file 'Abai Kunanbaev.jpg', cropped and downscaled.
portrait.creator: Unknown photographer

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: RISKY (Stage B) / LEAD SURVIVED WITH CAVEATS: the lead Commons file 'Abai Kunanbaev.jpg' has no creator, date or holder on its page (generic PD-old, 'from en.wiki', a 2020 crop with levels from a baq.kz news-page scan), and the Stage B note could not say whether it was the 1887 drawing or a photograph. I established that it is a crop of the famous photograph of Abai with his sons (a photograph, not a drawing; the Qalam article describes the sitter's frontal pose, vertical-striped chapan and skullcap, which the crop shows), and that the 1887 Lobanovsky drawing is a different, lifetime work reproduced only in a 2020 book (no file found). ROUTES TRIED (one bounded retry): (1) the lead as above; (2) the 1909 first edition on the World Digital Library/Library of Congress (Commons PDF pages 1-3 show a cover, title page and manuscript replacement leaf, no portrait; the WDL and loc.gov item pages are Cloudflare/403/503 walled and were not bypassed); (3) the 1887 Lobanovsky drawing (no accessible file or holder record); (4) the Semey regional library and Abai museum pages (domain not resolvable or not reached). The holder (Abai Museum, Semey) record was therefore NOT read; provenance rests on the Qalam article, which cites the museum receipt and a 1995 journal. The 1852 x 2460 earlier Commons version could not be downloaded (HTTP 429 from the upload server), so the current 1085 x 1460 version was used. RIGHTS: age-based and honest: no photographer or studio named in any source, creation no later than 1904, first publication undocumented (circulating from 1933, museum registration 1941); not claimed as PD on the Commons template alone. KIND likeness (a photograph of the sitter from life, late in life). INSCRIPTION/IDENTITY: no lettering on the crop; identity rests on the scholarly literature and museum registration, not on an inscription, and on the Commons file history; the crop cuts out the sons. QID VERIFIED LIVE (2026-11-18, Wikidata API) Q304890 label 'Abay Kunanbaiuly', description 'Kazakh poet, philosopher and composer (1845-1904)', instance of human, born 29 July 1845 (Wikidata; sources give 10 August), died 23 June 1904 (Bukeikhanov and Iskakov agree on the year; the Abai Institute's page says 1904), ko label 아바이 쿠난바이울리; no collision with an existing candidate or production slug. REGION central_asia (Kazakh steppe; precedent: Shokan Walikhanov and Alisher Navoi). ERA 19th_century. Nationality KZ (Wikidata says Russian Empire citizen). KOREAN NAME: the Wikidata Korean label 아바이 쿠난바이울리 was used as given; no other Korean source was checked, lead to confirm. ZERO POLITICS: primary identity is poet, translator and composer; his offices (volost head 1875-78, chief judge 1885), the 1885 legal regulations and his role as a precursor of the later Alash movement (a claim in a news article that was read but not used) are context only and not scored as politics; the Soviet-era use of him as an emblem of progress is context. ATTRIBUTION: limited_but_usable: much of what is written is from the Kazakh national and Soviet biographical tradition, the Auezov novels are literary, and only two accounts (Kennan 1891, Bukeikhanov 1905) are contemporary outside the family and circle; so only six rows are scored, at capped confidence. SOURCES READ (8 besides Wikidata): Kennan 1891 (the passage and context), Bukeikhanov 1905 (English translation, full), Abai Institute biography (full), Iskakov (full), Ozdemir (Turkish, full), Bashiri (full), Kazinform (relevant part), Qalam (about 70%, all of the portrait history). Also read but not cited: the e-history.kz library article, the qazaqculture America article, dknews, adebiportal. NOT OPENED OR BLOCKED: Britannica (404), Encyclopaedia Iranica, Auezov's novels and biography, Abai's own Words (no full English text opened), the Abai Museum records, WDL and loc.gov (walled), the Lobanovsky drawing. INDEPENDENT BEHAVIOURAL SOURCE FAMILIES: about 3 (Kennan; Bukeikhanov and the biographies derived from him; Ozdemir via the Kazakh literature textbook) plus the official Abai Institute family; Bashiri is a short Western summary; his own verse is self-report. NON-SELF BEHAVIOURAL SOURCES: Kennan, Bukeikhanov, Ozdemir. CONTRADICTIONS AND LIMITS: sources disagree on his religious observance (kept Ramadan but lax in prayer versus did not observe fasting), on whether he withdrew from public affairs (Bukeikhanov) or remained a leading arbiter (official biography), on birth date and place, and on the number of the Words; Kennan's account is hearsay that does not name Abai; the English texts of Bukeikhanov and Iskakov are rough translations; the Orazbai feud and the 1885 regulations rest on one official source and are not carded as fact beyond what is hedged. The rows are sparse (6) and will not meet the numeric match-eligibility floor, which is a match diagnostic and not an evidence defect. MAJOR ACHIEVEMENT GATE: cards are (1) written Kazakh literature and his verse, (2) the Russian translations, (3) the Words of Edification, hedged as official-biography-only.
